title: Steps from a minibatch
objectives: Explain how the batch size sets the noise in a gradient step, and pick a learning rate from a loss curve.

screens.title: Two hundred noisy gradients
screens.prose: Our net, a 2-16-16-2 tanh MLP, starts on 400 spiral points (two arms, `default_rng(0)`). The chart counts 200 minibatch gradients of its first weight, each from rows drawn at random with replacement. Batch 8 is shown.

params.xLabel: Minibatch gradient of the first weight

screens.question: Predict before you switch: at batch 128, how wide is the spread compared with batch 8?

options.text: About a quarter as wide
About a sixteenth as wide
options.why: You divided by $128/8 = 16$. The spread is a standard deviation, and it falls with the square root of the batch size.

options.text: About half as wide
options.why: Half would need four times the rows, batch 32. Batch 128 has sixteen times as many as batch 8.

options.text: Just as wide: the rows are the same rows
options.why: Each draw at 128 averages sixteen times as many rows, so more of their noise cancels.

hints.text: Each bar is a mean of the batch's row gradients.
Averaging $B$ independent numbers divides their sd by $\sqrt B$.
$\sqrt{128/8} = \sqrt{16} = 4$, so the spread is about a quarter.

feedback.correct: About a quarter: switch to batch 128 and the sd falls from 0.0140 to 0.0037.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Think about how an average of more rows behaves.

byKey.sixteenth: You divided by 16, the ratio of the batch sizes. The sd falls by its square root, 4.
byKey.same: More rows in each draw means more of their noise cancels.

explain.text: Sixteen times the rows gives $\sqrt{16} = 4$ times less spread. The two charts measure 0.0140 and 0.0037, a ratio of 3.78.

screens.title: An unbiased, noisy estimate
screens.prose: Name it: a batch drawn uniformly gives an **unbiased** estimate of the full gradient, here $-0.0019$, the mean over all 400 rows. When the $B$ rows are independent draws its sd is $\sigma/\sqrt B$. Across the 400 rows the first weight's gradient has $\sigma = 0.0409$.

params.xLabel: Minibatch gradient of the first weight

screens.question: What sd does that predict for batch 128? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: Divide $\sigma$ by the square root of the batch size.

byKey.over-b: You divided by 128. That is the variance rule; the sd divides by $\sqrt{128}$.
byKey.ratio: You divided by 16, the ratio of the two batch sizes, not by $\sqrt{128}$.

explain.text: $\sigma/\sqrt{128} = 0.0409/11.31 = 0.0036$. The chart's 200 draws give 0.0037, close to the prediction, as a sample sd of 200 should be.

screens.title: One step by hand
screens.prose: A one-weight model $\hat y = wx$ with loss $\tfrac12(wx - y)^2$ a row. A batch of three rows sits in the table. The batch gradient is the mean of $(wx - y)x$ over its rows.

state.caption: At $w = 1$. The batch gradient is the mean of the last column.

screens.question: At $w = 1$, take one SGD step with $\eta = 0.1$. What is the new $w$?

feedback.generic: Not quite. Average the last column, then step against it.

byKey.sum: You summed the column, $-9$. The batch gradient is the mean, $-3$, so the step is a third of that.
byKey.sign: You stepped with the gradient. SGD steps against it: $w - \eta g$.
byKey.one-row: You used the first row alone. The batch is all three rows.

explain.text: The mean of $-1$, $-2$ and $-6$ is $-3$. One step against it with $\eta = 0.1$ moves $w$ up by 0.3, to 1.3.

screens.title: The same rows, more steps
screens.prose: Two runs at $\eta = 0.5$, from the same start. Full-batch descent takes one step per epoch of 400 rows. SGD at batch 32 cuts each epoch into 12 batches of 32 and one of 16. The chart shows the full loss after each epoch.
screens.question: After 20 epochs both runs have seen 8,000 rows. How many steps has the SGD run taken?

hints.text: Count the batches in one epoch.
12 batches of 32 make 384 rows; the last 16 make a 13th.

feedback.correct: $20 \times 13 = 260$ steps, against 20 for full batch. Its loss is 0.142 against 0.438.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the steps in one epoch first.

byKey.epochs: That is the full-batch count, one step an epoch.
byKey.rows: You divided 8,000 by 32 and dropped the short batch at the end of each epoch.

explain.text: Each epoch is 13 steps, so 20 epochs are 260. For the same rows read, SGD took 13 times as many steps and ends at 0.142 against 0.438.

screens.title: A band, not a point
screens.prose: On a least-squares problem (1,000 rows, three features, `default_rng(7)`) SGD at batch 8 never settles on the minimum. The loss settles into a band above it. Slide the step size and read the mean excess loss.

state.caption: Step 0.05: mean excess over steps 101 to 300 is 0.0012

frames.caption: Step 0.05: mean excess over steps 101 to 300 is 0.0012
Step 0.1: mean excess over steps 101 to 300 is 0.0022
Step 0.2: mean excess over steps 101 to 300 is 0.0045
Step 0.4: mean excess over steps 101 to 300 is 0.0111

screens.question: What happens to the band as the step doubles?

options.text: Its height above the minimum roughly doubles
It halves, because bigger steps get there sooner
options.why: Bigger steps get near sooner, but then each noisy step also throws the weights further.

options.text: It stays the same: the noise comes from the batch, not the step
options.why: The batch sets the noise in the gradient; the step multiplies it into the weights.

options.text: It disappears once the step is large enough
options.why: The band grows with the step until the run diverges.

feedback.correct: Roughly: 0.0012, 0.0022, 0.0045 and 0.0111 as the step doubles.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the four captions in order.

byKey.same: The batch sets the gradient's noise, but every step scales it by $\eta$.

explain.text: Each step adds noise in proportion to $\eta$. The mean excess goes 0.0022 to 0.0045 from step 0.1 to 0.2, a factor of 2.0.

screens.title: Choosing the step from the curves
screens.prose: As in `makemore` l8, we sweep the step size and keep everything else fixed: 300 steps of batch 32 on the spiral net, five batch seeds per step size. The bars show the mean final full loss. At 2 and 4 (not drawn) the runs were unstable.

state.caption: After 300 steps of batch 32. Above 1.5 the runs turned unstable (not drawn).

screens.question: Which step size would you carry on with?

options.text: 0.5, the lowest of the steady runs
2, where a few runs ended lower still
options.why: At 2 the runs are unstable: rerun the same seed with arithmetic rounded a little differently and it lands somewhere else.

options.text: 0.1, because it is the safest of them
options.why: It is safe and slow: after 300 steps it is still at 0.383.

options.text: Whichever run had the lowest last minibatch loss
options.why: One minibatch is a noisy sample of the loss; compare full losses, as these bars do.

hints.text: Above 1.5 the runs were not steady enough to trust.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Take the lowest bar among the steady runs.

byKey.two: A rate at the edge of stability gives results that depend on luck and rounding, not on the rate.
byKey.last: Compare full losses on fixed rows, not the last batch.

explain.text: The sweep says 0.5: mean 0.141. Larger steps first get worse, then unstable: at 4 most seeds blew up, and at 2 a seed's result changed when only the rounding changed.

screens.title: Is a smaller batch worse?
screens.prose: Ana says batch 8 must be worse than batch 128, since each of its gradients is noisier. Both runs use $\eta = 0.5$ and are plotted per epoch, so each point is the same number of rows read.
screens.question: What does the chart say?

options.text: Per row read, batch 8 is ahead after one epoch: 50 steps against 4
Ana is right: batch 128 is lower from the first epoch
options.why: Read the first epoch: 0.444 for batch 8 against 0.487 for batch 128.

options.text: They must be equal per row read, since both read the same rows
options.why: The same rows give batch 8 thirteen times the steps.

options.text: Batch 128 wins per step, so it wins
options.why: Per step, yes; but a step of 128 rows costs sixteen of 8.

hints.text: Look at epoch 1 on both lines.
Batch 8 takes 50 steps an epoch; batch 128 takes 4.
More steps per row read can beat less noise per step, early on.

feedback.correct: After one epoch batch 8 is at 0.444 and batch 128 at 0.487; after 20, 0.083 and 0.380.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read both lines at the same epoch.

byKey.ana: That is the misconception: noise per step is not cost per row. Batch 8 took 50 steps in the epoch batch 128 took 4.

explain.text: Noisier steps, but far more of them for the same rows: after 20 epochs batch 8 is at 0.083 and batch 128 at 0.380. Per step, a larger batch is better; per row read, early on, it often is not.

screens.title: Step and batch together
screens.prose: The noise a step adds to the weights is about $\eta \cdot \sigma/\sqrt{B}$, so the step size and the batch size set it together. A heuristic from large-batch image training, the **linear scaling rule**, grows $\eta$ in proportion to $B$, after a warm-up and only up to a limit. It is a starting point, not a law: check it with a sweep.
screens.question: A run uses batch 32 at $\eta = 0.05$. What step does the linear scaling rule suggest for batch 256?

feedback.correct: $256/32 = 8$, so $0.05 \times 8 = 0.4$, to be checked with a sweep.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Scale $\eta$ by the same factor as $B$.

byKey.sqrt: Scaling by $\sqrt 8$ is another rule some use; the linear rule scales by 8 itself.
byKey.inverse: You divided by 8. A larger batch is less noisy, so the rule allows a larger step.

explain.text: The batch is 8 times larger, so the rule scales the step by 8 to 0.4. It holds only while the step is small enough to be stable; past that, a sweep decides.

screens.title: Minibatches in code
screens.prose: Write `minibatch_indices(n, B, seed)`: one epoch, a permutation from `np.random.default_rng(seed)` cut into batches of `B` (the last may be short). Write `sgd_step(params, grads, lr)` returning new arrays. Then `grad_spread(B, trials, seed)`: with one generator, draw each batch by `rng.integers(0, len(Xr), B)` and return the sample sd of the batch means.
screens.question: Complete the three functions.

widget.prelude:
import numpy as np
_g = np.random.default_rng(7)
Xr = _g.standard_normal((1000, 3))
yr = Xr @ np.array([1.5, -2.0, 0.5]) + 0.5 * _g.standard_normal(1000)


def grad_rows(w):
    # one gradient row per data row: (x . w - y) x, the gradient of 0.5 (x . w - y)^2
    return (Xr @ w - yr)[:, None] * Xr

tests.call: [a.tolist() for a in sgd_step([np.array([1.0, 2.0]), np.array(3.0)], [np.array([0.5, -1.0]), np.array(2.0)], 0.1)]

widget.how: Submit runs 9 hidden tests. `Xr`, `yr` and `grad_rows(w)` are loaded. Tests 1 to 3 check one epoch of batches exactly and that it covers every row once. Tests 4 and 5 check `sgd_step` and that it leaves its inputs alone. Test 6 runs five steps and compares the weights exactly. Test 7 compares `grad_spread` exactly on a seed, and tests 8 and 9 compare it with $\sigma/\sqrt B$ within 5% and 10%.

mutants.symptom: Draws rows with repeats, so an epoch misses some rows.
Updates the arrays in place, changing the caller's parameters.
Steps up the gradient instead of down.
Sums the batch instead of averaging it, so the spread grows with B.

hints.text: `order[i:i + B]` for `i` in `range(0, n, B)` cuts the epoch.
A list comprehension `[p - lr * g ...]` builds new arrays.
In `grad_spread`, take column 0 of `grad_rows(np.zeros(3))` once, then index it by each batch.

feedback.correct: All pass. On these rows $\sigma = 3.0239$, so batch 64 should give about 0.3780.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Read the first failing test in the results.

screens.title: A million rows of returns
screens.prose: A desk fits a return model on 1,000,000 daily rows. A full-batch step reads every row, so it trains on minibatches instead, and its loss curve looks ragged. The gradient of one coefficient has sd 0.8 across rows.
screens.question: Taking draws as independent, what batch size brings that coefficient's gradient sd down to 0.01?

feedback.correct: $\sqrt B = 0.8/0.01 = 80$, so $B = 6{,}400$: still under 1% of the rows a full step reads.

byKey.no-square: You found $\sqrt B = 80$ and stopped. Square it.
byKey.variance: You divided 0.64 by 0.01, mixing a variance with an sd.

explain.text: $0.8/\sqrt{B} = 0.01$ gives $\sqrt{B} = 80$ and $B = 6{,}400$. A batch that size costs 0.64% of a full step, and the ragged curve is the band this lesson measured.

ideas: A batch drawn uniformly gives an unbiased estimate of the gradient. With independent draws its sd is $\sigma/\sqrt{B}$: four times the rows halves it.
At a fixed step, SGD settles into a band above the minimum whose height grows with the step; per row read, small batches often win early.
Pick the step from a sweep of final full losses: the lowest among the steady runs, here 0.5. Near the edge of stability, results turn to luck.

formula.name: Minibatch noise
formula.note: Rows drawn independently; $\sigma$ is the sd of one row's gradient.

summary.trap: A noisier step is not a worse run: compare runs per row read, by the full loss, not by one minibatch.

quiz.prose: A minibatch gradient has sd 0.02 at batch 16. The rows are independent draws.
quiz.question: What is its sd at batch 64?

feedback.correct: Four times the rows halves the sd: $0.02/\sqrt 4 = 0.01$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The sd falls with $\sqrt{B}$.

byKey.linear: You divided by 4. The sd falls by $\sqrt 4 = 2$.
byKey.up: A larger batch has less spread, not more.

explain.text: $64/16 = 4$ and $\sqrt 4 = 2$, so the sd halves to 0.01.

quiz.prose: The batch size equals the data set, 400 rows, drawn without replacement.
quiz.question: How noisy is the step?

options.text: Not noisy: every batch is the whole set, plain descent
As noisy as $\sigma/\sqrt{400}$, the rule for 400 rows
options.why: That holds for independent draws with replacement. Without replacement, 400 of 400 rows is always the same batch.

options.text: As noisy as batch 1, which reads one row a step
options.why: Batch 1 is the noisiest choice; the whole set has no noise.

options.text: Half as noisy as batch 100, four times smaller
options.why: With every row in every batch there is nothing left to vary.

feedback.correct: No noise at all: the edge case where SGD is plain gradient descent.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What changes from one batch to the next?

explain.text: Drawn without replacement, a batch of all 400 rows is the same every time. The step is the full gradient, with no noise.

quiz.prose: A data set has 50,000 rows and a batch holds 64; the last batch of an epoch may be short.
quiz.question: How many steps make one epoch?

feedback.correct: $50{,}000/64 = 781.25$, so 781 full batches and one short one: 782 steps.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Divide and count the short batch.

byKey.floor: You dropped the short last batch of 16 rows.
byKey.rows: That is batch 1, one row a step.

explain.text: $781 \times 64 = 49{,}984$, leaving 16 rows for a 782nd, shorter batch.

quiz.prose: Batch size 1: each step uses one row.
quiz.question: Which is true?

options.text: Unbiased, with the largest spread a batch can have: sd $\sigma$
The step is biased, because one row cannot stand for the data
options.why: One row drawn uniformly is still an unbiased estimate; it is just noisy.

options.text: It always trains fastest, because it takes the most steps
options.why: More steps per row, but each is noisy; at a large step the band can swamp the progress.

options.text: It is plain gradient descent with a small step
options.why: Plain descent uses every row each step; batch 1 uses one.

feedback.correct: Batch 1 is unbiased and as noisy as it gets: sd $\sigma$ a step.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Is a single uniform row biased?

explain.text: A uniform row has the full gradient as its mean, so the step is unbiased. Its sd is $\sigma/\sqrt 1 = \sigma$, the largest a batch can have.
